claims.claim: In Ontario, the lakes moose used heavily were shallower, with mineral-rich sediment (Fraser et al. 1984, abstract only)
claims.location: Abstract (PDF p. 2); Results 'Characteristics of heavily and lightly used lakes' (PDF p. 9); Discussion (PDF p. 11)
claims.quote: heavily used sites had shallower water, a higher mineral content in the lake sediment
claims.conditions: Sibley Provincial Park, Ontario (north shore of Lake Superior), 24 lakes and ponds, 1976–80: 6 heavily used, 16 lightly used, 2 unclassified (use rated from trails and 3-h watches); mean depth 0.7 ± 0.4 m vs 1.8 ± 1.2 m (P < 0.01); 'mineral content' was measured as LESS ORGANIC MATTER (loss on ignition) in sediment under < 2 m of water: 28 ± 15 % vs 47 ± 16 % organic (P < 0.05); preferred plant species covered 11 ± 10 % vs 3 ± 10 % of the < 2-m bottom
claims.note: now read in full, so '(abstract only)' can go. 'Mineral-rich' should be read as 'inorganic (clay or silt, less organic) sediment', not sediment rich in sodium or other minerals; the authors attribute the preference to more productive, phosphorus-richer plants on inorganic beds, not to firmer footing

claims.claim: sodium-rich plants and shallow lakes preferred (Fraser et al. 1984)
claims.location: Abstract (PDF p. 2); Results (PDF pp. 8–9); Table 1 (PDF p. 5)
claims.quote: Preferred species had significantly higher sodium content.
claims.conditions: a 'cafeteria' experiment beside a well-used lake, 19 aquatic species offered (Table 1), plants harvested 6 June–23 July 1979: 7 preferred (eaten completely every time), 7 intermediate (29–80 % eaten), 5 unpreferred (0–15 %); preferred species higher in sodium than intermediate or unpreferred (P < 0.05); heavily used lakes shallower (0.7 vs 1.8 m mean depth)
claims.note: the same comment line's 'in New Hampshire belly-deep on yellow pond-lily' is not from Fraser et al. (a Sibley, Ontario study; the research note credits the Forest Society) — keep it outside this citation

notes: Important for the sim's moose diet (plants3.js MOOSE preference by species): in this cafeteria test Characeae (stoneworts) were eaten 0 ± 0 % in 4 presentations and water horsetail (Equisetum fluviatile) 5 ± 9 %, both in the UNPREFERRED class, with Eleocharis acicularis (15 %), Potamogeton robbinsii (4 %) and Typha latifolia (0 %); Nuphar variegatum was intermediate (72 ± 37 %). The seven preferred (100 % eaten) were Myriophyllum verticillatum, Utricularia vulgaris, Potamogeton gramineus, P. epihydrus, P. filiformis, P. foliosus and Scirpus subterminalis (Table 1, PDF p. 5). This contrasts with Isle Royale's 58 % stonewort diet (Belovsky & Jordan 1978), and §3.8.4's closing remark that stoneworts are the only plants collected in the Hot Brook lakes should be read against it. Other values: aquatic plants far richer in sodium and iron than woody browse; plants from heavily used lakes higher in Na, P and Mn; three heavily used lakes had the fastest flushing (3, 11, 60 d); Sibley moose numbered 100–200 in the 243-km² park; aquatic feeding fell off after mid-July, and the authors judge Sibley moose not as sodium-short as Isle Royale's (summer browse ~50 ppm Na vs 5–30 ppm).
